To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the electron density distributions in the laser plasma near a plane target were calculated for various residual gas pressures, and the conditions for the propagation of an optical breakdown near the target were analyzed.
Two-exposure holographic interference was used to study evolution of laser plasma near a copper target as a function residual gas (argon or helium) pressure.
the propagation of an optical plasma near a target is possible at a pressure of ~ 10-2 torr and that it is impossible at a pressure of 10-4 torr.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of the theory of optical discharge in a gas, with the study of its properties, with the development of methods of its diagnostics and with the study of the conditions under which the discharge can propagate near a solid surface.
the study of the early stages of the evolution of a laser discharge near a target as well as the conditions for propagation of the optical discharge.

the development of a new method of laser plasma diagnostics and with the investigation of the early stages of the evolution of a laser-induced plasma near a target in the case of a laser pulse of nanosecond duration.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the optical breakdown in a gas is a threshold phenomenon.
the optical discharge is a very important phenomenon in laser-plasma interactions and should be taken into account in the interpretation of the experimental results.
the propagation of the optical discharge is possible only at the pressures of the residual gas lower than a critical value.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the optical breakdown threshold for a laser intensity of ~1011 W/cm 2 is 0.01-1 Torr for helium, and 0.1-10 Torr for argon.

the optical discharge propagates along the laser beam axis, the electron density distribution is nonuniform, and there are no significant differences in the plasma evolution in the case of argon and helium.

in the case of laser radiation intensities of ~1011 W/cm 2, the optical breakdown of the gas occurs at a pressure of ~10-2 Torr and the optical discharge propagates in the gas at pressures of 0.5-10 Torr.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the laser-induced plasma can be used as a source of high-intensity ultrashort laser pulses.

the propagation of an optical dis- charge near a target is a very complex process, and the conditions for this process are determined by the parameters of the laser pulse, the target, the ambient gas, and its interaction with the plasma.
the optical discharge propagates near the target at a pressure of 1.3 Torr of argon and 1.0 Torr of helium, which corresponds to the "breakdown" threshold for a laser intensity of 1011 W /cm2.
